Q: Who is Dr. Saffi Velloquin and what is her expertise in endocannabinoid medicine?
A: Dr. Saffi Velloquin is a synthetic guest, invented for this test fixture. In the episode she is described as a phytopharmacist and women's health strategist who studies how the endocannabinoid system meets female-specific physiology, and her segment turns that science into steps a listener can take this week.

Q: What is the endocannabinoid system and how does it affect perimenopause symptoms like mood, sleep, and brain fog?
A: The endocannabinoid system (ECS) is a signaling network found throughout the body whose job is balance: it helps regulate sleep, mood, pain and the menstrual cycle. Dr. Velloquin explains that estrogen and the ECS influence each other, so when estrogen swings in perimenopause, ECS tone can swing with it. That is one reason sleep, mood and focus can all feel unsettled at once.

Q: What is anandamide and why does it drop during perimenopause?
A: Anandamide — from the Sanskrit word for "bliss" — is an endocannabinoid produced on demand in your body, and its function closely mirrors that of THC: it binds to CB1 receptors to reduce pain perception and improve mood. Dr. Velloquin explains that estrogen directly promotes anandamide production, which is why women typically feel better and have higher pain tolerance around ovulation when estrogen peaks. In perimenopause, as estrogen oscillates erratically rather than declining in a straight line, anandamide levels become equally unpredictable — stripping away the rhythmic mood and pain regulation that premenopausal women rely on without even realizing it. Understanding this link is the first step toward targeting ECS support intentionally during the perimenopause transition.

Q: What does chronic high-THC cannabis use do to the endocannabinoid system in perimenopausal women?
A: Chronic high-dose THC overstimulates the ECS — a finely tuned balancing system — until receptor sensitivity downregulates and the system essentially stops responding, which Dr. Velloquin describes as the body saying "I'm not going to accept this anymore." Women are hit harder than men because they metabolize THC into stronger metabolites that stay in the body longer due to higher fat cell percentages, and after three to four days of use, women show significantly higher plasma THC levels than men at the same dose. Dr. Velloquin recommends that no one needs flower above 20% THC, and that any THC-containing products should be used in the late evening — never during the day — to avoid further impairing cognitive function that is already under stress during perimenopause.

Q: What is the simplest thing a perimenopausal woman can do today to support her endocannabinoid system naturally?
A: Look at the balance of omega-3 and omega-6 fats in your diet, because those fats are the raw material the body uses to make its own endocannabinoids. Dr. Velloquin suggests adding oily fish or a good-quality omega-3 supplement and cutting back on heavily processed seed oils, and checking with your clinician before you start anything new.
